\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\title{Candidate Alloys for a Pedestrian Bridge Deck: Screening Report}
\author{Materials Selection Group}
\date{July 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
Four candidate alloys were screened for a pedestrian bridge deck.
Density, modulus, yield strength, elongation, conductivity, and cost were measured.
Steel remains the baseline against which all candidates are judged.
Titanium leads on strength but fails the cost screen.
Brass offers a middle path for decorative elements.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
The pedestrian bridge at Riverside Park needs a new deck structure.
The existing timber deck has reached the end of its service life.
The city asked for a metal replacement with a forty-year design life.
Four candidate alloys were shortlisted by the materials selection group.
The shortlist came out of a broader screening of twelve alloys.
Screening criteria included strength, stiffness, weight, and cost.
Corrosion resistance was assessed in a parallel study.
This report covers the mechanical and economic measurements only.
The deck panels are simply supported between steel stringers.
Panel spans reach 1.8 m in the longest bays.
Pedestrian loading follows the municipal bridge code.
Occasional maintenance vehicles add a concentrated wheel load.
Weight matters because the existing stringers stay in place.
Heavier panels would force stringer strengthening.
Stiffness governs the vibration comfort of pedestrians.
Yield strength governs the ultimate capacity checks.
Thermal conductivity matters for surface temperature in summer.
Barefoot use is common near the park playground.
Cost is normalized against structural steel as the baseline.
The city procurement office caps the normalized cost at 2.0.
Any candidate above that cap needs a written waiver.
The screening results feed directly into the concept design review.
\section{Specimens}
All four alloys were sourced as hot-rolled plate.
Plate thickness was 12 mm across the board.
Coupons were cut by waterjet to avoid a heat-affected zone.
Tensile coupons followed the lab flat-coupon standard.
Three coupons per alloy were tested.
Density was measured by the Archimedes method.
Each density value is the average of three weighings.
The steel came from the same mill as the original stringers.
The aluminum was a 5083 marine-grade plate.
The titanium was grade 5, chosen for its strength.
The brass was a naval brass plate.
Surface finish was kept as-rolled for all coupons.
Coupons were degreased before testing.
Ambient temperature in the lab stayed near 21 degrees.
Humidity was not controlled but stayed moderate.
All measurements were taken within one week.
The same technician ran every test.
Calibration records for the instruments are on file.
\section{Test Methods}
Tensile testing followed the lab standard operating procedure.
Crosshead speed was 2 mm per minute up to yield.
Extensometer readings captured the elastic modulus.
Yield strength was read at the 0.2 percent offset.
Elongation was measured over a 50 mm gauge length.
Fractured coupons were photographed for the record.
Thermal conductivity came from a guarded hot plate rig.
Discs of 50 mm diameter were machined for that rig.
Each conductivity value is the average of two discs.
Cost index values came from current supplier quotes.
Quotes were normalized to the steel quote per kilogram.
Fabrication cost differences were not included at this stage.
They will enter the comparison at concept design.
Test data were logged straight into the lab database.
Outliers were checked against the raw curves.
No data points were discarded.
The modulus values agreed with handbook values within 6 percent.
The yield values sat slightly below handbook values.
That gap is typical for hot-rolled plate.
Full stress-strain curves are archived with this report.
The rig uncertainty was estimated at plus or minus 4 percent.
Uncertainty bars are omitted from the summary table for readability.
\section{Quality Assurance}
All instruments held valid calibration certificates.
The tensile frame was verified with reference blocks.
The hot plate rig passed its daily check before each session.
Raw data were backed up at the end of each day.
A second engineer spot-checked the database entries.
Two entries were corrected after that review.
Both corrections involved transposed digits in elongation values.
The corrected values appear in the summary table.
No other anomalies were found.
The review log is archived with the raw data.
Supplier quotes were confirmed in writing.
Quote validity extends through the end of the year.
Currency fluctuations within that window are ignored.
The screening protocol itself was audited last year.
\section{Results}
All measurements passed the quality checks described above.
The four alloys spanned a wide range of properties.
Titanium was the strongest and the most expensive by far.
Aluminum was the lightest and the best conductor.
The table below collects the measured values.
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Measured properties of the four candidate alloys. Density in g/cm$^3$, modulus in GPa, yield strength in MPa, elongation in percent, conductivity in W/(m K), cost normalized to steel.}
\label{tab:properties}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Material & Density & Modulus & Yield & Elongation & Conductivity & Cost \\
\midrule
Steel & 7.85 & 200 & 250 & 18 & 50 & 1.0 \\
Aluminum & 2.70 & 69 & 95 & 12 & 167 & 1.4 \\
Titanium & 4.51 & 116 & 880 & 10 & 22 & 6.8 \\
Brass & 8.73 & 110 & 340 & 25 & 120 & 1.9 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The values in the table feed the scoring matrix used at concept design.
Raw curves and quote sheets are archived with this report.
Any rerun requested by the review panel can reuse the same coupons.
\section{Discussion}
Steel remains the reference point for every criterion.
Its low cost keeps it competitive despite its weight.
Aluminum saves about two thirds of the weight per panel.
Its lower modulus raises a vibration concern at long spans.
A deeper panel section could recover the lost stiffness.
That change would eat into the weight saving.
Titanium clears every mechanical bar with room to spare.
Its cost index sits far above the procurement cap.
A waiver for titanium is unlikely to survive review.
Brass lands between aluminum and steel on most axes.
Its conductivity is high enough to stay cool in summer sun.
Its strength is adequate for the governing load case.
The decorative railing already uses a brass finish.
Matching the deck alloy would simplify detailing.
Galvanic pairing with the steel stringers needs checking.
Isolation pads would handle that risk.
Drainage details will differ across the alloys.
Standing water on the deck shortens coating life.
The next stage should model panel vibration explicitly.
Fatigue from pedestrian traffic deserves a dedicated check.
The corrosion study will report next quarter.
Its results could reorder the ranking.
For now the scoring matrix favors aluminum and brass.
Steel stays in the running on cost grounds alone.
\section{Conclusion}
Four alloys were screened on six measured criteria.
The measurements passed all quality checks.
Titanium leads on strength and fails on cost.
Aluminum leads on weight and conductivity.
Brass offers the best balance for this application.
Steel remains the fallback on cost.
The scoring matrix will rank the candidates at concept design.
Panel vibration and fatigue checks come next.
The review panel meets in September.
This report is the main input to that meeting.
The final selection is due at the autumn review.
\end{document}

instruction: results 那章的合金表太宽了，指标全挤在一行，打印出来肯定顶到页边。这样处理：你先数数它的数据列（材料名那列不算），超过 5 列就把整张表转置——指标变行、材料变列，首列表头写成 Property；要是没超过，就保持行列不变，在表末尾加一列算每种材料的均值。两种情况只做一种，别多也别少。caption、label 和三线表样式都保留，数字一个都不许抄错。
